processing: A steamed green tea: heat from steam stops oxidation, which is rare among Yunnan greens, and the leaf is then shaped and dried. It uses improved Yunnan large-leaf varieties.
harvest_season: Little is recorded about picking dates for this tea. As with most Chinese greens, spring leaf is normally the most prized.
appearance_dry: Tight, rounded, firmly made leaf with a faint frosty bloom on the surface.
appearance_wet: As with other steamed large-leaf greens, expect soft green leaf, somewhat broader than that of small-leaf Chinese greens.
taste_profile: Fresh and savoury-sweet with a clean finish, and an aroma sold in several styles: sweetcorn, chestnut or plain clean-green.

brewing.notes: A starting point typical of steamed greens, not a documented recipe for this tea. Large-leaf material turns brisk fast in hotter water, so go cool and short first.

vintage_note: Sold like other green teas, as a recent harvest meant to be drunk fresh rather than aged. Lots are not usually tracked by year in the way pu-erh is, so check the production date on the pack and pass on anything old.
description:
Zhengmei is a steamed green tea from Yunnan, best known from Gengma county in Lincang. Yunnan's greens are usually overshadowed by its pu-erh and black tea, and most Chinese greens are pan-fired or baked, so a steamed tea made from big-leaf bushes is an unusual thing.

The name points to the step that defines it: steam knocks out the leaf's enzymes and keeps the colour green. Large-leaf Yunnan varieties are the raw material, which is what separates it from the small-leaf steamed teas of Japan.

In the cup it should be bright green and fresh, with a savoury sweetness. Makers sell it in aroma styles described as sweetcorn, chestnut and clean-green. As with other steamed greens, water that is too hot is the usual mistake; keep it around 80 °C.

Much of what is on record comes from one Gengma producer group and its Huiwei brand, whose line runs from silver-needle grades to broken green tea. Treat its descriptions as a maker's account of its own tea, and look for a recent production date when buying.
history:
Gengma's steamed green tea is documented mostly through its local producer, Yunnan Gengma Zhengmei Tea Group, whose own account says its Huiwei brand became a Yunnan provincial famous trademark in October 2003. When the style began is not clearly recorded.

Lincang as a whole is described as a birthplace of Yunnan steamed large-leaf green tea. The producer also reports sales around China and to Japan and Myanmar.
